Bhubaneswar

Lingaraja Temple

The great Shiva temple of Bhubaneswar, which scholars call the most notable temple in Odisha. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Panigrahi: 'by far the most notable temple not only of Bhubaneswar, but also of Orissa'. Brown: 'the finest living example of the Orissan group'.

Meet the temple

At first the temple had only the tower shrine and its porch. The dance hall and the offering hall were added later. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,2]

Panigrahi explained that a temple's chief god came to be seen as living like a king. So the god needed an audience hall, a dance hall and a dining hall. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

According to a temple chronicle, a queen had the eastern part of the temple rebuilt. Panigrahi thought she was Queen Kolavati, mother of Uddyota Kesari, and that she most likely built the porch hall. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [2]

For curious grown-ups

The chronicle (Madala Panji, as quoted by Panigrahi) names her Tulavati Rani, wife of Vasukalpa Kesari. Panigrahi calls it 'most probable' that she was Kolavati, the builder of the Brahmesvara temple, and says she was the queen of Yayati II. Both steps are his inferences.

The main temple rises straight from the ground, with no high plinth (raised base) under it. Panigrahi contrasted this with the Parvati temple, which stands on a high plinth. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

When?

11th century CE Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2,3]

How do we know?

Scholars date the main temple to the 11th century CE.

Brown: c. 1000 CE. Panigrahi: 11th century, most probably begun c. 1020–1040 CE and completed c. 1040–1065 CE. No foundation inscription is known; the dating is stylistic and indirect.

In whose time?

Somavamshi (Kesari) Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

How do we know?

The main temple was built in the time of the Somavamshi (Kesari) kings.

Panigrahi treats 'Kesari' and 'Somavamshi' as the same kings. He says the side halls were later additions, possibly of the Ganga period.

For which god?

Shiva as Tribhuvanesvara (Lingaraja) Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

How do we know?

The temple is dedicated to Shiva. Hindus worship him here as Tribhuvanesvara, also known as Krittivasa and Lingaraja.

Temple type?

pancharatha deul Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

How do we know?

According to K.C. Panigrahi, the main shrine is a pancharatha deul.

The temple stands in a very holy area. Percy Brown noted that the many temples in and around Bhubaneswar show how sacred this place was. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [3]

No known inscription names the builder. Historian K.C. Panigrahi thought it most likely that King Yayati II began it and his son Uddyota Kesari finished it. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [2]

For curious grown-ups

This is one scholar's inference, not proven. Panigrahi (1961) dates Yayati II c. 1020–1040 CE and Uddyota Kesari c. 1040–1065 CE, and calls the attribution 'most probable'. He credits Yayati I with the Mukteshvara temple, not with Lingaraja. Some popular accounts name Yayati I instead; no accepted source for that has been checked.

Historian K.C. Panigrahi thought this temple replaced an older temple on the same spot. Some early sculptures in the courtyard may have come from that older temple. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

According to tradition, King Sasanka built an earlier temple at this shrine in the 7th century CE. Panigrahi could not identify which temple that was. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [2]

For curious grown-ups

Four Sanskrit texts credit Sasanka with a temple in this shrine. Panigrahi accepts that a stone temple stood here in the early 7th century CE. He dates the present temple to the 11th century and says the earlier temple cannot be identified.

How it was built

Step 1

James Fergusson noted that the tower is built wholly of stone, from base to top. He also wrote that every stone in it has a carved pattern. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

Step 2

The tower is hollow inside. R.D. Banerji saw rooms stacked one above another, reached by a stair built inside the thick wall. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

Step 3

The temple stands in a walled courtyard about 158 m by 142 m (520 by 465 ft). The thick outer wall is made of laterite blocks. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2,3,4]

Stop 3 of 4

The parts

More to spot

Today Lingaraja has all four buildings of a fully developed Odisha temple: the tower shrine, the porch hall, the dance hall and the offering hall. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [3]

Many smaller shrines crowd the courtyard around the main temple. Percy Brown compared this to Buddhist shrines grouped around a great stupa. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [3]

Panigrahi wrote that the temple dominates the landscape for miles around. He called it the purest example of the Kalinga style of building. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

See 1 more

When Ganga kings later remodelled the temple, they added some features linked to Vishnu. Panigrahi noted these are not found in other Shiva shrines. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

Stop 4 of 4

Its family

Panigrahi found the main shrine closely related in design to the Brahmesvara temple. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

Panigrahi wrote that later Ganga kings tried to match or outdo the builders of Lingaraja. They built even grander temples at Puri and Konark. Percy Brown noted that Puri follows the same four-building plan, in one line. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2,3]
